extracted.intended_audience: Members of Congress, congressional staff, DOD managers, procurement/policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for applying OMB Circular A-76 and the FAIR Act to decide whether recurring federal commercial activities should be performed in-house or outsourced via managed competitions, with emphasis on DOD implementation and oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of commercial activity / recurring commercial activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A commercial activity is one that is a result of a requirement that the federal government has for a product or service and that the product or service could be obtained from a private sector source. A 'recurring' commercial activity is one that is required by the federal government on a consistent, long-term basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to determine whether an activity is potentially subject to outsourcing under A-76; distinguishes temporary or unique functions from those suitable for competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of managed competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The three types of managed competitions under the policy are (1) public-public, (2) public-private, and (3) private-private.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions are the vehicle for cost-comparison studies to decide who best performs the work; competitions may pit government MEOs against private contractors or other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeframes for completing competitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory guidance directs that single-function competitions are to be completed within 24 months and multi-function competitions within 48 months; GAO reports multi-function studies since 1991 averaged about 30 months.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness is a performance criterion; both proponents and opponents agree the A-76 process often takes too long, and duration affects the realization of projected savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to develop a Performance Work Statement (PWS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal executive agencies are required to develop a performance work statement, defining the technical aspects of the work to be performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PWS serves as the basis for fair comparison across bidders and the MEO; inadequate requirement definition is an identified procurement weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to determine the Most Efficient Organization (MEO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must determine the most efficient organizational structure using the current government workforce (called the 'Most Efficient Organization' or MEO) through realignment/reexamination of management structure, personnel requirements and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MEO is the in-house benchmark used in cost comparisons; often the government reorganizes employees into an MEO prior to competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to conduct cost-comparison studies among all sectors
rubrics_metrics.description: When such a comparison is required, agencies must conduct cost-comparison studies among all sectors, including private contractors, other public agencies, and the in-house MEO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost-comparison studies are the analytic framework for deciding 'who best to do the work'; however, certain conversions/waivers may exempt some activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy assumption: government should not compete against citizens
rubrics_metrics.description: The policy rests on the assumption that the federal government should not compete against its citizens but rely on the commercial sector to supply needed products and services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative assumption underpins A-76 but is contested; it affects decisions about what to put up for competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy assumption: market forces and self-managed competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assumes the government can use market forces to determine effective and cost-efficient methods and that competition within the marketplace can be 'self-managed' without requiring government oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These assumptions inform the policy’s reliance on private-sector competition; critics dispute whether market/self-management assumptions hold in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overhead and bidding parity guidance (administrative/overhead rates and win margin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government routinely assigns 12-13% administrative and overhead costs for competing federal agencies; outside proposals must be at least 10% less than the MEO’s proposals to win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private sector contests this low overhead rate (IT community cites ~40%); critics argue the 12-13% rate and 10% win margin may bias competitions in favor of the government.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIR Act inventory annual reporting requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal executive agencies are required to submit to OMB, by June 30 of each year, annual inventories (lists) of 'non-inherently governmental functions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventories are published and made available to Congress and the public; inventories are the starting point for considering which activities to subject to managed competitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of inherently governmental functions (OFPP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inherently governmental functions include activities requiring exercise of discretion in applying Government authority or making value judgments for the Government; examples include acts of governing, determining/protecting/advancing U.S. interests, significantly affecting life/liberty/property, commissioning/appointing/directing employees, and exerting ultimate control over government property or funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions not considered inherently governmental are deemed commercial and subject to competitive outsourcing; ministerial tasks (e.g., mail, housekeeping, facilities ops) are typically excluded from being inherently governmental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory challenge and resolution process (FAIR Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency inventory lists can be challenged by 'interested parties'; once challenged, agencies must accept the challenge, make changes, or reject it and do so within 30 days. OMB will review and publish lists in the Federal Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenge procedures create oversight and public scrutiny; initial inventories took longer due to opportunity for appeals and OMB review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions and exclusions to FAIR / A-76
rubrics_metrics.description: Exceptions to the FAIR Act include entities such as GAO, government corporations/government-controlled corporations, non-appropriated fund instrumentalities, and certain depot-level maintenance organizations; the Supplemental Handbook allows for direct conversion to private contractors and cost-comparison waivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all functions listed as commercial will be subject to competition; legal/procedural exceptions affect scope and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and implementation variability across agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: A-76 has not been used uniformly: DOD has been the lead user, while many civilian agencies relied on re-invention, re-engineering, and consolidation instead of conducting A-76 studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Variation in agency practices affects overall government-wide impact and complicates oversight and comparative assessment of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of projected savings (GAO skepticism and measurement of costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO found DOD’s estimates of savings may be overstated because costs of conducting competitions and investment costs were not fully calculated and competitions have taken longer than projected, delaying savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realizing savings requires accounting for upfront competition costs, realistic timelines, and detailed plans; failure to do so can lead to overstated projections and budgetary misplanning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procurement/contract management performance criteria (IG audit findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: DoD Inspector General audit found recurring contract management problems: non-use of prior history to define requirements, inadequate government cost estimates, cursory technical reviews, inadequate competition, failure to award multiple-award contracts, inadequate price negotiation memoranda, inadequate contract surveillance, and lack of cost control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These implementation deficiencies are criteria for assessing the quality and reliability of A-76 competitions and subsequent contract performance; they are anti-patterns that undermine expected savings and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact on workforce and need to retain certain organic capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Managed competitions can result in the loss of thousands of federal jobs; evidence shows MEOs sometimes operate more efficiently than contractors, and agencies should retain organic, technical capability for unique requirements (e.g., computerized engineering, nuclear propulsion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions should weigh workforce impacts, mission-critical capabilities, safety, training, and loyalty considerations—not only short-term cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: National security and mission impact considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Outsourcing certain functions (e.g., weapons handling) may compromise national security because of concerns about training, strikes/work stoppages, oath/loyalty differences, and contractor-driven cost decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functions that significantly affect safety, security, or mission readiness require heightened scrutiny and may be excluded from competitive sourcing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to A-76 (strategic sourcing and other reorganization tactics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives include restructuring, re-engineering, consolidation, termination of inefficient practices, strategic sourcing (systemwide analysis under which services can modify jobs and keep them without managed competitions), and other measures that allow services to meet savings goals without traditional A-76 contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies may pursue alternatives to achieve projected savings more quickly or flexibly, but Congress and oversight bodies should ensure cost/benefit analyses accompany such alternatives to avoid arbitrary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional oversight and reporting obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress can exercise oversight by monitoring agency progress in implementation of A-76 policy and FAIR, determining whether reported cost savings are real, and granting agencies authority to explore alternatives to A-76. Agencies must meet deadlines and report promptly, accurately, and completely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight is essential to ensure inventories, challenges, and competitions are conducted in both the letter and spirit of the law; reporting transparency (publication in Federal Register, OMB website) supports audit and review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement and reporting of competition outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, about 60% of competitions were won by the original employing agency reconfigured into an MEO and 40% by private contractors; more recent results had shifted with private contractors winning about 60% and government agencies 40%. DOD projected potential savings of roughly 20-30% from competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome statistics and realized savings should be tracked and validated; shifts in win rates affect expected workforce and budgetary impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge escalation and legal remedies risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggrieved bidders and other parties may seek legal remedies if inventory or competition decisions are disputed; if not handled expeditiously, challenges can lengthen procurement cycles, increase rule-making, and expand judicial/regulatory involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural clarity and timely resolution of disputes are important to prevent delays and unintended oversight by courts or regulators.
